newsitem.title: ARGENTINA: Argentina to investigate past as Nazi haven.
newsitem.headline: Argentina to investigate past as Nazi haven.

text.p: Argentina is setting up a commission to investigate its role as a haven for Nazi war criminals, including reports that gold stolen from Holocaust victims was hidden here, the government said on Thursday.

The commission of Argentine and foreign experts set up by President Carlos Menem will "look into the infiltration of Nazis into Argentina and so-called Nazi gold," Foreign Minister Guido Di Tella said. "It will have a year to carry out its investigations and elaborate a final report."

Argentina is eager to shake off its image as a haven for Nazi war criminals on the run after the war and has opened Central Bank archives for Jewish investigators trying to track down gold stolen from Jewish victims of the Holocaust.
Recently declassified U.S. wartime documents from 1945 estimate that the Nazis secretly sent more than $1 billion to be invested in Argentina one month before the war ended.

Nazi hunters of the Simon Wiesenthal Centre have also called for an investigation into allegations that the Argentine government gave thousands of blank passports to Nazis fleeing Europe on the orders of President Juan Peron.

Peron, president from 1946-55 and 1973-74, was an admirer of Italian fascist ruler Benito Mussolini. During his first period in power, Argentina was the refuge for some top Third Reich officials including Hitler's confidante Martin Bormann, Holocaust "architect" Adolf Eichmann and possibly Auschwitz concentration camp doctor Josef Mengele.
The country also attracted many Jewish immigrants and has one of the biggest Jewish communities in the world.

Its open-door policy to Nazis has been given a new airing by the trial of former SS Capt. Erich Priebke in Italy for the 1994 Ardeatine Caves massacre. Priebke lived openly in Argentina under his own name until his extradition in 1995.
Argentine Interior Minister Carlos Corach told a news conference the new committee would be "one more step" on the way to atoning for past mistakes.

"It is indispensable that we clarify what happened in Argentina in the last years of World War II and the postwar with regard to investments and political influences etc. among sectors linked to the Nazi regime," he said.
